kc.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen, Pereira, Raes and Smith, 1998), Chapter 6, Table 12, Winter Wheat. https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
kc.assumption: Table 12 prints an initial value of 0.4 with frozen soils and 0.7 with non-frozen soils, and an end value of 0.25 to 0.4 where the higher value is for hand-harvested crops. The tool uses the frozen-soil value, 0.4, and the lower end value, 0.25. Both are the tool's own choices.

stageDays.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 11, Winter Wheat planted in October, Idaho, USA (335 days). https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
stageDays.assumption: Table 11 has three winter wheat rows: California, the Mediterranean and Idaho. The tool uses the Idaho row, the one planted in October, and stretches or shrinks the four stages in proportion so that they fill the usual Kansas season in calendar.json. The choice of row is the tool's own. FAO-56 calls these lengths a general guide.

heatSensitiveMonths.source: K-State Wheat Production Handbook (C529, May 1997): "High-temperature damage is most apparent during grain filling"; it also names "the high temperatures of June". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/C529.pdf
heatSensitiveMonths.assumption: The handbook names the stage and June's heat in separate places. The tool treats June as the sensitive month.

nFixing.source: UC Davis, Growing Rice with Less Fertilizer: "Cereal plants like rice and wheat don't have that capability." https://www.ucdavis.edu/food/news/growing-rice-with-less-fertilizer

residue.source: K-State, The Value of Crop Residue (MF2604, October 2003): "Wheat is a large residue producer". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/download/value-of-crop-residue_MF2604 ; USDA NRCS, Nebraska Conservation Planning Sheet No. 4, Crop Residue Management (revised December 2006): high residue crops include small grains. https://www.mssoy.org/sites/default/files/documents/residue-mgmt-nrcs-2006.pdf

rootDepth.source: K-State, Soil, Water, and Plant Relationships (L904, December 2014), Table 2: depth of root penetration for wheat, 4 to 6 feet. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/L904.pdf
rootDepth.assumption: The table gives depths, not classes. The tool calls a crop deep-rooted only when the table's range goes beyond 6 feet, which among these crops is alfalfa; the others are medium.

kc.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 12, Maize, Field (grain). https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
kc.assumption: The initial value 0.3 is printed for the cereals group, not on the maize row. The end value is printed as 0.60 to 0.35: 0.60 for harvest at high grain moisture and 0.35 for harvest after the grain has dried in the field. The tool uses 0.35.

stageDays.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 11, Maize (grain) planted in April, Spain (spring, summer) and California (150 days). https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
stageDays.assumption: Table 11 has six maize rows. The tool uses this one and scales the four stages in proportion to the usual Kansas season in calendar.json. FAO-56 calls these lengths a general guide.

heatSensitiveMonths.source: K-State Corn Production Handbook (C560, September 2007): under hot, dry stressful conditions pollination can be poor or incomplete. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/C560.pdf ; USDA NASS Kansas Crop Progress, weeks ending 12 and 19 July 2026: the statewide five-year average of corn silking was 45 and then 60 percent. https://www.nass.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Statistics_by_State/Kansas/Publications/Crop_Progress_and_Condition/2026/KS-weekly0713.pdf and https://www.nass.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Statistics_by_State/Kansas/Publications/Crop_Progress_and_Condition/2026/KS-weekly0720.pdf
heatSensitiveMonths.assumption: K-State names the stage, not a month. The tool takes the month in which USDA's statewide five-year average for silking passes half of the crop, which is July.

nFixing.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln research news: "Corn and other crops can't, requiring nitrogen fertilizers to maximize growth and yield." https://research.unl.edu/blog/husker-scientist-leads-effort-to-understand-adapt-legume-nitrogen-conversion/

residue.source: USDA NRCS, Nebraska Conservation Planning Sheet No. 4, Crop Residue Management (revised December 2006): "High residue crops include corn, grain sorghum, forage sorghum and other summer forage crops, and small grains." https://www.mssoy.org/sites/default/files/documents/residue-mgmt-nrcs-2006.pdf

rootDepth.source: K-State, Soil, Water, and Plant Relationships (L904, December 2014), Table 2: depth of root penetration for corn, 4 to 6 feet. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/L904.pdf
rootDepth.assumption: The table gives depths, not classes. The tool calls a crop deep-rooted only when the table's range goes beyond 6 feet, which among these crops is alfalfa; the others are medium.

kc.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 12, Sorghum, grain. https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
kc.assumption: The initial value 0.3 is printed for the cereals group, not on the sorghum row. The mid-season value is printed as 1.00 to 1.10. The tool uses the middle of that range, 1.05.

stageDays.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 11, Sorghum planted in May or June, USA, Pakistan and the Mediterranean (130 days). https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
stageDays.assumption: Table 11 has two sorghum rows. The tool uses the one that names the United States and scales the four stages in proportion to the usual Kansas season in calendar.json. FAO-56 calls these lengths a general guide.

heatSensitiveMonths.source: K-State Grain Sorghum Production Handbook (C687, revised May 1998): "Planting should be timed so flowering avoids the hottest, driest period of summer." https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/C687.pdf ; USDA NASS Kansas Crop Progress, weeks ending 2 and 9 August 2026: the statewide five-year average of sorghum headed was 38 and then 55 percent. https://www.nass.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Statistics_by_State/Kansas/Publications/Crop_Progress_and_Condition/2026/KS-weekly0803.pdf and https://www.nass.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Statistics_by_State/Kansas/Publications/Crop_Progress_and_Condition/2026/KS-weekly0810.pdf
heatSensitiveMonths.assumption: K-State names the stage, not a month. The tool takes the month in which USDA's statewide five-year average for heading passes half of the crop, which is August.

nFixing.source: K-State, Soil Test Interpretations and Fertilizer Recommendations in Kansas (MF2586, January 2024): it prints a fertilizer nitrogen recommendation for grain sorghum, with a minimum of 30 pounds of nitrogen per acre. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/MF2586.pdf
nFixing.assumption: No source opened says in so many words that sorghum fixes no nitrogen. K-State treats it as a crop that needs nitrogen fertilizer, so the tool records it as not nitrogen-fixing.

residue.source: USDA NRCS, Nebraska Conservation Planning Sheet No. 4, Crop Residue Management (revised December 2006): "High residue crops include corn, grain sorghum, forage sorghum and other summer forage crops, and small grains." https://www.mssoy.org/sites/default/files/documents/residue-mgmt-nrcs-2006.pdf ; K-State, The Value of Crop Residue (MF2604, October 2003): "If the previous crop was sorghum or wheat, and a high level of residue is in place". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/download/value-of-crop-residue_MF2604

rootDepth.source: K-State, Soil, Water, and Plant Relationships (L904, December 2014), Table 2: depth of root penetration for grain sorghum, 4.5 to 6 feet. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/L904.pdf
rootDepth.assumption: The table gives depths, not classes. The tool calls a crop deep-rooted only when the table's range goes beyond 6 feet, which among these crops is alfalfa; the others are medium.

kc.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 12, Soybeans. https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
kc.assumption: The initial value 0.4 is printed for the legumes group, not on the soybean row. The mid-season and end values are the soybean row's own.

stageDays.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 11, Soybeans planted in May, Central USA (140 days). https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
stageDays.assumption: The table prints the development stage as 30/35; the tool uses 35, the value that adds up to the printed total of 140 days. The four stages are scaled in proportion to the usual Kansas season in calendar.json. FAO-56 calls these lengths a general guide.

heatSensitiveMonths.source: K-State, 2022 Kansas Performance Tests with Soybean Varieties (SRP1173, January 2023): "The pod setting marks the beginning of the most critical period of the crop". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/2022-kansas-performance-tests-with-soybean-varieties_SRP1173.pdf ; USDA NASS Kansas Crop Progress, weeks ending 2 and 9 August 2026: the statewide five-year average of soybeans setting pods was 37 and then 52 percent. https://www.nass.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Statistics_by_State/Kansas/Publications/Crop_Progress_and_Condition/2026/KS-weekly0803.pdf and https://www.nass.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Statistics_by_State/Kansas/Publications/Crop_Progress_and_Condition/2026/KS-weekly0810.pdf
heatSensitiveMonths.assumption: K-State names the stage, not a month. The tool takes the month in which USDA's statewide five-year average for setting pods passes half of the crop, which is August.

nFixing.source: K-State Soybean Production Handbook (C449, October 2016): "Under normal conditions, soybeans need no nitrogen fertilizer as the nodule bacteria will fix sufficient nitrogen". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/C449.pdf

residue.source: K-State, The Value of Crop Residue (MF2604, October 2003): "scheduling corn to follow soybean (a low residue crop)". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/download/value-of-crop-residue_MF2604 ; USDA NRCS, Nebraska Conservation Planning Sheet No. 4, Crop Residue Management (revised December 2006): low residue crops include soybeans. https://www.mssoy.org/sites/default/files/documents/residue-mgmt-nrcs-2006.pdf

rootDepth.source: K-State, Soil, Water, and Plant Relationships (L904, December 2014), Table 2: depth of root penetration for soybeans, 5 to 6 feet. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/L904.pdf
rootDepth.assumption: The table gives depths, not classes. The tool calls a crop deep-rooted only when the table's range goes beyond 6 feet, which among these crops is alfalfa; the others are medium.

kc.source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 6, Table 12, Alfalfa Hay, averaged cutting effects. https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e0b.htm
kc.assumption: Table 12 has three alfalfa rows. The tool uses hay with the effects of cutting averaged over the season, not a single cutting period and not alfalfa grown for seed.

nFixing.source: K-State Alfalfa Production Handbook (C683, revised October 1998): "Rhizobium bacteria, present on well-nodulated alfalfa, can fix enough nitrogen to meet the needs of the growing alfalfa crop." https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/C683.pdf

rootDepth.source: K-State Alfalfa Production Handbook (C683, revised October 1998): "Alfalfa is a deep-rooted, drought-tolerant perennial". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/C683.pdf ; K-State, Soil, Water, and Plant Relationships (L904, December 2014), Table 2: depth of root penetration for alfalfa, 6 to 10 feet. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/L904.pdf
